title: Patience and the Prayer of Faith

verses.text: Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you.
Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes.
Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire. You have hoarded treasure in the last days.
Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.
You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter.
You have condemned and murdered the righteous, who did not resist you.
Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord's coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains.
You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord's coming is near.
Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged. Look, the Judge is standing at the door!
Brothers, as an example of patience in affliction, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.
See how blessed we consider those who have persevered. You have heard of Job's perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath. Simply let your "Yes" be yes, and your "No," no, so that you will not fall under judgment.
Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises.
Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.
And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.
Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.
Elijah was a man just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years.
Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops.
My brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back,
consider this: Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins.

context.author: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (1:1). Tradition identifies him with James the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem.
context.genre: Letter with the feel of wisdom literature and a sermon
context.audience: Probably Jewish Christians living outside the land of Israel (“the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” 1:1). Some take the phrase as a title for all of God's people.
context.setting: James denounces rich people who have hoarded wealth and withheld wages. He then calls believers to patience until the Lord’s coming, like a farmer waiting for rain. He gives instructions for prayer for the sick, praying elders, anointing with oil, and confession, with Elijah as an example.
context.custom: Farmers in Israel counted on the early rains of autumn, which let them plant, and the late rains of spring, which filled the grain (Deuteronomy 11:14). Oil was used for healing (Luke 10:34), and the Twelve anointed the sick with oil (Mark 6:13). “Do not swear” (v.12) repeats Jesus' teaching (Matthew 5:34-37).
context.timelineImmediate: The letter ends abruptly with a call to restore wandering believers.
context.timelineBible: Job is the example of steadfastness (v.11) and Elijah of prayer (1 Kings 17-18). “Lord of Hosts” (v.4) is a prophetic title (Isaiah 5:9). To “cover over a multitude of sins” (v.20) is close to Proverbs 10:12.
context.sparkNotes: Come now, you rich, weep and howl. Your wealth has rotted and the wages of your laborers cry out. Be patient until the coming of the Lord, like the farmer waiting for the precious fruit of the earth. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job. Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone sick? Let him call for the elders, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil. The prayer of faith will save the one who is sick. The prayer of a righteous person has great power. Elijah prayed, and it did not rain.

translation.meaning: Can mean heal, rescue, or save.

otBackground.note: Elijah announced that there would be no rain (James 5:17).
The Lord restores Job. James 5:11 points to this outcome.
Love covers all offenses. Compare James 5:20.

overview.summary: James warns the rich, calls believers to patience until the Lord comes, and encourages prayer for the sick and for restoring wanderers.

history.t: The Law said a day laborer must be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:14-15; Leviticus 19:13). James says the wages that were held back are crying out (5:4), as Abel's blood did (Genesis 4:10).

First Kings 17-18 tells how Elijah prayed for drought and for rain. James says it did not rain for three and a half years (5:17), and Luke 4:25 gives the same figure. First Kings 18:1 says the rain came in the third year, so the numbers are counted in different ways.

customs.t: Olive oil was used on wounds (Luke 10:34), and the Twelve anointed many sick people with oil (Mark 6:13). James tells the elders to pray over the sick person and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord (5:14). Whether the oil is medicine, a sign, or both is debated.
The early rain of autumn softened the ground for planting, and the late rain of spring filled out the grain (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24). A farmer could do nothing to hurry them.
In Jesus' day people backed their words with oaths by heaven, the temple or the altar (Matthew 5:33-37; 23:16-22). James repeats the command to let a plain yes and no be enough (5:12).

archaeology.t: A limestone tablet from Gezer, from about the 10th century BC, lists the farm tasks of the year in order. It shows the yearly round that a farmer in these hills lived by.

A pottery fragment of the 7th century BC from a Judean fort on the coast records a reaper's complaint that an official took his garment. It is much older than James, but it shows a harvest worker appealing for justice.
Stone presses found at sites around the Mediterranean show how olive oil was made. It was used for food, for light and for healing.

overview.discussion: James says the prayer of a righteous person has great power. Whom could I pray for today, and what keeps me from doing it?
overview.book: The letter of James · 5 chapters. Brisk, practical teaching in the tradition of Proverbs and the Sermon on the Mount.
overview.author: James

historicalImage.caption: A pottery fragment from the 7th century BC, found in 1960 at a Judean fortress near Yavne-Yam on the coast and now in the Israel Museum. In it a field worker complains to the commander that an official took his garment after he finished his harvesting, and asks for it back. It is some six centuries older than James, but it shows a harvester appealing for justice, as the workmen do in James 5:4.

currentImage.caption: The view from the rooftop lookout of the Muhraqa Carmelite monastery on Mount Carmel, with Haifa at the far left and Megiddo to the right. Muhraqa, a name that means the burning place, is the traditional place of Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). The Bible does not name the exact spot on the long Carmel ridge. James 5:17-18 recalls Elijah's prayers for drought and for rain.
